How do new ideas and inventions change the way people live, and who gets the credit?
invention. A new thing or a new way of doing something that solves a problem. Example: the light bulb.
inventor. A person who makes an invention.
patent. A government paper that says an invention belongs to its inventor. For a set time, others can't copy it without permission.
engineer. A person who uses science and math to design and build things.
mathematician. A person who is an expert in math.
astronaut. A person who is trained to travel into space.
abolitionist. A person who worked to end slavery.
An invention is a new thing or a new way to solve a problem. Inventors start with a problem. They try an idea, test it and make it better. Many inventions change how people live every day.

Let me follow one invention. Problem: long ago, homes were dark at night. People used candles and oil lamps. They were smoky and could start fires. Idea: an electric light bulb. But early bulbs burned out fast. Inventors kept testing. Lewis Latimer and others found better ways to make the thin part inside that glows. Bulbs lasted longer and cost less.

Ellen Ochoa is an engineer. Her problem: how can a computer "see" and check objects? Her idea: use light . She and her team tested ways for computers to spot objects and clean up blurry pictures. They got patents for these inventions. Every inventor follows the same steps: find a problem, try an idea, test it, make it better.

Benjamin Franklin was a printer, an inventor and a founder of the United States. He signed the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. He also enslaved people for many years. Later, he worked to end slavery. Historians tell the whole story.

A historian lists what Franklin did, good and bad. He invented the lightning rod to keep houses safe from fires. He started a library and a fire company in Philadelphia. But for many years, he enslaved people in his home. Later in life, he changed his mind. In 1787, he became the leader of a group working to end slavery. Both parts are true.

A poster says: "Ben Franklin was a great inventor." Is it true? Yes, but it is not the whole story. A better poster says: "Ben Franklin was an inventor and a founder. He enslaved people for many years. Later, he worked to end slavery." Now the poster tells what he really did.
Big inventions are often made by teams . But sometimes only one name gets remembered. Some builders were left out because they were Black, women or both. Historians look for the hidden people too.

I ask: who else helped? Thomas Edison is famous for the light bulb. But many people worked on it. Lewis Latimer was a Black inventor. He taught himself to draw plans. He made the drawings for Alexander Graham Bell's telephone patent . He helped make light bulbs better. Later he taught English and drawing to immigrants . For many years, his name was left out of books.

In 1953, Katherine Johnson started work at a research center in Virginia. It later became part of NASA. At first, Black women there had to work in a separate office . That was unfair. Still, her math was so good that astronauts trusted it. For years, few people knew her name. In 2015, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom .

Franklin wrote: as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours; and this we should do freely and generously. In plain words: We get a lot of help from other people's inventions. So we should be glad to help others with our inventions. We should share them freely. Facts: Franklin said no to the patent for his stove. He did not patent the lightning rod or his other inventions either. Other people were free to make and sell his stove.

Benjamin Franklin. Franklin is also known for bifocals , glasses with two kinds of lenses in one frame. He wrote Poor Richard's Almanack , a yearly book with weather, sayings and tips. He enslaved people for many years. In 1790, near the end of his life, he asked Congress to end slavery.

Lewis Latimer. Lewis Latimer was born free in Massachusetts. His parents had escaped slavery in Virginia. As a teen, he served in the U.S. Navy . Then he worked for patent lawyers and taught himself to draw plans. In 1890, he wrote a book about electric lighting. He also taught English and drawing to immigrants .

Katherine Johnson. Katherine Johnson grew up in West Virginia . She loved to count everything. She finished high school at 14 and college at 18. At NASA, she did math by hand for space flights. In 2017, NASA named a building after her.

Mae Jemison. Mae Jemison grew up in Chicago. She studied to be an engineer and a doctor. She worked as a doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia in West Africa. In 1992, she flew on the Space Shuttle Endeavour . She was the first Black woman in space.

Ellen Ochoa. Ellen Ochoa grew up in California. Her family has roots in Mexico . She is an engineer and an inventor . She has patents for ways computers use light to check objects. In 1993, she became the first Hispanic woman in space. She even played her flute there! Later, she led NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.
